lead: An equilibrium equation talks about forces on one body. So cut that body free of everything touching it and replace each support by the force it gives. That drawing is the free body diagram (FBD). Every statics problem — a lamp on a ceiling, a signboard on a bracket, a block on a ramp — starts here. Get the diagram right and the rest is arithmetic.
prereq: You need Chapter 1.3 (resolving forces) and Chapter 1.4 (adding forces at a point).

blocks.text: Newton's laws apply to a chosen body. They say nothing about the supports. Remove those supports and replace each by the force it gave the body. What remains is the free body: the body alone, with arrows for every external force on it.

This follows from Newton's third law. If a wall pushes a block, the block pushes the wall back equally. Only the wall's push acts on the block. The other force belongs on the wall's diagram. One diagram, one body.
A free body diagram is that drawing. Each arrow carries a label, a direction and a magnitude, or a symbol if unknown. The equations of Chapter 1.6 are written straight from the arrows.

items: Choose the body: a block, ring or knot. If a rope tension is asked, the knot may be easier than the block.
Draw the body alone, a simple outline. No walls, floor, or rope drawn as an object.
Add the weight W = mg, straight down, at the centroid. m is mass in kg; g = 9.81 m/s². Weight never tilts with a slope.

Replace each support by its reaction. A smooth surface gives a normal reaction N, perpendicular to the surface. A rope gives tension T along the rope, away from the body. A pin gives two unknown components.
Add every applied load: hanging weight, push, pull, wind.
Check the count. Every arrow must have a named source, and every support you cut must appear as an arrow.

blocks.text: Most marks are lost by forgetting one support, not by slipping on signs.

sections.h3: What never appears on the diagram

items: Internal forces: tension inside a single rod, force between the two halves of one body.
Forces the body exerts on others: the block's push on the plane, the rope's pull on the ceiling. These belong on the other body's diagram.
The support itself — the wall, floor, pin or rope drawn as an object. Once you cut the support away, the support is gone from the picture and only the reaction force it gave remains as an arrow.

blocks.text: The inclined plane is the classic test. A block rests on a plane tilted at angle θ to the horizontal. The normal reaction is perpendicular to the sloped surface, so it makes angle θ with the vertical. The weight stays vertical. Many students draw the weight along the slope; it never is.
W = mg, N ⊥ surface, T along the rope
blocks.where: W is weight in N, m is mass in kg, g = 9.81 m/s², N is the normal reaction in N perpendicular to the smooth surface, T is tension in N acting away from the body along the rope. Ropes pull only; smooth surfaces push only.

blocks.text: Choose axes. On a slope, take x along the plane and y perpendicular to it. Resolve every arrow onto these axes, as in Chapter 1.3. Then write ΣFx = 0 and ΣFy = 0 for a particle at rest, as in Chapter 1.6. Two equations, two unknowns at most.
Rigid bodies and moments come in Unit 2. Friction on an incline comes in Unit 3.

figure.caption: Follow the arrows down: the body is chosen, supports are cut away, weight and reactions are added, and the last box checks that every arrow has a source.

spec.aria: A six-step flowchart: choose the body, cut it free, add the weight, replace each support by a reaction, add ropes and loads, then count the arrows.

examples.question: A block of mass 10 kg rests on a smooth plane inclined at 30° to the horizontal. A string parallel to the plane holds it from sliding down. Take g = 9.81 m/s². Draw the free body diagram and find the tension in the string and the normal reaction from the plane.
steps: Body: the block. Cut away the plane and the string.
Forces on the block: weight W = mg = 10 × 9.81 = 98.1 N, vertically down; normal reaction N, perpendicular to the plane; tension T, up the plane along the string.
Axes: x along the plane (positive up the slope), y perpendicular to the plane (positive away from it).
The weight makes 30° with the negative y axis. Its components are W sin 30° down the slope and W cos 30° into the plane.
Along the plane: T − W sin 30° = 0, so T = 98.1 × 0.5 = 49.05 N.
Perpendicular to the plane: N − W cos 30° = 0, so N = 98.1 × 0.8660 = 84.96 N.

Check: T is along the plane and N is perpendicular, so T ⊥ N and together they balance W. T² + N² = 49.05² + 84.96² = 2406 + 7218 = 9624 = 98.1² = W². Agrees. Equivalently, T = W sin 30°, N = W cos 30°, and the squares add to W².
examples.answer: Tension T = 49.05 N up the plane and normal reaction N = 84.96 N perpendicular to the plane.
examples.check:
import math
m = 10.0
g = 9.81
theta = math.radians(30.0)
W = m * g
T = W * math.sin(theta)
N = W * math.cos(theta)
print(round(W, 2))
print(round(T, 2))
print(round(N, 2))

examples.question: A lamp of mass 4 kg hangs from a knot where two ropes meet. One rope runs horizontally to a wall, the other runs at 40° above the horizontal to the ceiling. Take g = 9.81 m/s². Find both rope tensions.
steps: Body: the knot, not the lamp. The lamp hangs from the knot by a short rope.

Forces on the knot: the downward pull of the lamp's rope, equal in magnitude to the lamp's weight W = mg = 4 × 9.81 = 39.24 N; tension T1 in the horizontal rope, pointing away from the knot (left); tension T2 in the inclined rope, pointing away at 40° above the horizontal.
ΣFx = 0: T2 cos 40° − T1 = 0, so T1 = T2 cos 40°.
examples.answer: T2 = 61.05 N in the inclined rope and T1 = 46.77 N in the horizontal rope.
examples.check:
import math
m = 4.0
g = 9.81
ang = math.radians(40.0)
W = m * g
T2 = W / math.sin(ang)
T1 = T2 * math.cos(ang)
print(round(W, 2))
print(round(T2, 2))
print(round(T1, 2))

traps: Drawing the force the block presses on the plane. That arrow belongs on the plane's diagram.
Drawing the weight along the incline. Weight is always vertical; only its components lie along and across the slope.
Forgetting the weight of a light-looking body, or adding it twice when rope and block are one body.
Making a rope push. Tension pulls away from the body; a negative T means the rope would go slack.
Taking the normal reaction as vertical on an inclined plane. It is perpendicular to the surface, so it tilts by the same angle as the plane.

quiz.q: State what a free body diagram shows and what it leaves out.
quiz.a: It shows one chosen body alone, with arrows for every external force on it: weight, support reactions and applied loads. It leaves out the supports themselves, internal forces, and every force the body exerts on other bodies.

quiz.q: Why does the push of a block on an inclined plane not appear on the block's free body diagram?
quiz.a: That push acts on the plane, not the block. By Newton's third law it is the equal and opposite partner of the normal reaction N that the plane gives the block. Only N acts on the block, so only N is drawn.

quiz.q: A rope and a smooth floor both touch a body. Explain why one reaction is drawn along the rope and the other perpendicular to the floor.
quiz.a: The rope can only pull along its length, so its tension T points away from the body along the rope. The smooth floor can only push, and with no friction it pushes only perpendicular to its surface, so N is drawn perpendicular to the floor.

quiz.q: A 5 kg block hangs from a single vertical rope. Take g = 9.81 m/s². Draw the free body diagram of the block and find the tension.
quiz.a: Two forces: weight W = 5 × 9.81 = 49.05 N down, tension T up. ΣFy = 0 gives T = 49.05 N.

quiz.q: A 20 kg block sits on a smooth plane inclined at 25°. Take g = 9.81 m/s². Find the normal reaction.
quiz.a: W = 20 × 9.81 = 196.2 N. Perpendicular to the plane: N = W cos 25° = 196.2 × 0.9063 = 177.8 N. No string is mentioned, so the block would slide; the question asks only for N.

quiz.q: A student draws a block on an incline with weight W along the slope, a normal reaction vertical, and a friction force up the slope. Identify the errors and state the correct diagram for a smooth plane.
quiz.a: Weight must be vertical, not along the slope. The normal reaction must be perpendicular to the plane, not vertical. Friction on a smooth plane is zero, so no friction arrow exists. Correct diagram for the smooth case: two arrows — W vertical down and N perpendicular to the plane — plus the string tension up the plane only if the question mentions a string.

quiz.q: Two blocks touch each other and rest on a smooth floor. Explain why the contact force between them cannot appear on a diagram of both blocks treated as one body, and what changes if they are drawn separately.
quiz.a: Treated as one body, the contact force is internal: it is an action-reaction pair inside the chosen body, so it cancels and is not drawn. Drawn separately, each diagram gets one of the pair — block 1 gets the push from block 2, block 2 gets the equal and opposite push from block 1 — and the two diagrams must be solved together.

beyond: Not for the exam. Free body diagrams come first in engineering simulation: structural software such as STAAD or ANSYS still asks for supports and loads in diagram form before building a stiffness matrix. In robotics, each link of an arm gets its own free body diagram before the equations of motion are written. Search for 'free body diagram of a link', 'reaction forces in a truss joint' or 'constraint forces in multibody dynamics' to go further.
